title: Gamble v. State
description: Whether Christopher Coy Gamble's custodial statement should be suppressed as the product of a pretextual arrest, and whether the precedent set by State v. Sullivan regarding pretextual arrests should be overruled.
plaintiff_argument: Gamble argued his custodial statement was obtained through an unlawful pretextual arrest and should be suppressed, and that the precedent of State v. Sullivan should not be overruled.
defendant_argument: The State argued Gamble's arrest was not pretextual, or if it was, the exclusionary rule did not apply, and in supplemental briefing, argued that State v. Sullivan should be overruled.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's denial of Gamble's motion to suppress and his motion to strike the venire, and overruled State v. Sullivan.

title: State v. Good Day Farm Arkansas
description: Whether the General Assembly has the authority to amend voter-initiated constitutional amendments, specifically Amendment 98, and whether the germaneness requirement in section 23(a) refers to "section" or "amendment."
plaintiff_argument: The General Assembly lacks authority to amend voter-initiated constitutional amendments without a public vote, as per the precedent of Arkansas Game & Fish Commission v. Edgmon, and any legislative amendments must be germane specifically to section 23 of Amendment 98, not the entire amendment.
defendant_argument: The General Assembly has the authority to amend voter-initiated laws with a two-thirds vote under article 5, section 1 of the Arkansas Constitution, and the word "section" in section 23(a) of Amendment 98 was a drafting error and should be read as "amendment" to apply to the entire amendment.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's ruling, holding that the General Assembly has the authority to amend voter-initiated laws like Amendment 98 and that the germaneness requirement applies to the entire amendment, not just section 23, and explicitly overruled Arkansas Game & Fish Commission v. Edgmon.

title: Land v. BAS, LLC
description: Whether the Commissioner of State Lands provided constitutionally adequate notice to BAS, a California LLC, before selling its Arkansas property to recover delinquent property taxes, with BAS arguing notice was inadequate and the Commissioner arguing it was sufficient.
plaintiff_argument: BAS argued that the Commissioner failed to provide constitutionally adequate notice of the tax sale, violating its due process rights and constituting an unlawful taking, thus sovereign immunity should not apply.
defendant_argument: The Commissioner argued that the notice provided to BAS was constitutionally sufficient, and therefore, BAS failed to raise a valid claim that would overcome sovereign immunity.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's decision, ruling that the Commissioner's notice was constitutionally sufficient and sovereign immunity applies, thus granting summary judgment to the Commissioner.

title: Spencer v. State
description: Whether a circuit court's gag order, intended to ensure a fair trial, violates constitutional rights to free speech and due process by being overly broad, vague, and lacking factual basis.
plaintiff_argument: The gag order violates his due-process rights to a fair and public trial and his First Amendment right to speak, as it is an unjustified prior restriction on speech.
defendant_argument: The gag order is within constitutional limits, protects the integrity of the case, and ensures a fair trial for both parties.
decision_outcome: The court granted the petition for writ of certiorari, issued the writ, and vacated the circuit court's gag order.

title: McGill v. Thurston
description: Whether the popular name and ballot title for a proposed constitutional amendment concerning the Pope County casino license are sufficient and not misleading to voters.
plaintiff_argument: The popular name and ballot title are insufficient and misleading because they fail to disclose crucial information, misrepresent the revocation of an existing license, incorrectly restrict future amendments, do not comport with the text regarding voter majority, and fail to disclose conflicts with federal law.
defendant_argument: The popular name and ballot title are sufficient, intelligible, honest, and impartial, accurately reflecting the proposed amendment's scope and import, and do not contain misleading tendencies or partisan coloring.
decision_outcome: The court denied the petitioners' request to remove the measure from the ballot.

title: Paschall v. Thurston
description: Whether the popular name and ballot title for the proposed "Medical Marijuana Amendment of 2024" are sufficient and not misleading to voters.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners, Bill Paschall and Arkansans for Patient Access (APA), argued that the ballot title of the proposed constitutional amendment was sufficient and requested that votes for it be counted.
defendant_argument: The respondent, John Thurston (Secretary of State), initially argued that APA failed to meet the minimum-signature requirement, while the intervenors, Jim Bell and Protect Arkansas Kids (PAK), argued that the popular name and ballot title were misleading.
decision_outcome: The court denied the petitioners' request, denied the respondent's request, and granted the intervenors' request, enjoining the Secretary of State from canvassing or certifying ballots for the proposed amendment.

title: Thurston v. The League of Women Voters of Arkansas
description: Whether four acts (736, 973, 249, and 728 of 2021) passed by the Arkansas General Assembly, which regulate various aspects of the election process, violate the Arkansas Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Acts violate equal protection, free and equal election clauses, voter qualifications, and free speech/assembly clauses by making it substantially harder for voters to obtain absentee ballots, shortening deadlines, enacting strict voter identification, and impeding nonpartisan voter support activities, thereby disenfranchising voters.
defendant_argument: The Acts are constitutional and were enacted to advance compelling governmental interests of protecting the integrity of Arkansas elections, preventing fraudulent voting, and promoting public confidence in election security.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the circuit court's decision, holding that the four Acts (736, 973, 249, and 728 of 2021) are not clearly incompatible with the Arkansas Constitution, and dismissed the case.

title: Arkansas Department of Education v. Jackson
description: Whether the emergency clause of the LEARNS Act was validly enacted by the General Assembly, with the appellees arguing it was not due to a lack of a separate roll-call vote, and the appellants arguing it was, as evidenced by legislative journals.
plaintiff_argument: The emergency clause of the LEARNS Act was invalid because the General Assembly failed to pass it by a separate roll-call vote as required by the Arkansas Constitution.
defendant_argument: The LEARNS Act emergency clause received a separate roll-call vote, and the legislative journals serve as the official record confirming its proper adoption.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the circuit court's ruling, finding that the legislative journals are the sole evidence for the proper adoption of the emergency clause, and dismissed the case.

title: Eddie Armstrong & Lance Huey v. Thurston
description: Whether Arkansas Code Annotated section 7-9-111(i) is constitutional and whether the ballot title for a proposed constitutional amendment to legalize adult-use cannabis is sufficient.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that section 7-9-111(i) is unconstitutional because it grants the State Board of Election Commissioners discretion over ballot title certification, violating the Arkansas Constitution, and that their ballot title is sufficient.
defendant_argument: The respondents and intervenors argued that section 7-9-111(i) is constitutional as it facilitates the ballot-title review process, and that the ballot title is insufficient due to misleading omissions regarding THC dosage limits, child-protection measures, industrial-hemp effects, facility tiers, and the definition of "adult."
decision_outcome: The court granted the petition, ruling that Arkansas Code Annotated section 7-9-111(i) is unconstitutional and that the proposed ballot title is sufficient, ordering the Secretary of State to certify it for the November 8, 2022 general election ballot.

title: Arkansas Department of Finance & Administration v. 2600 Holdings, LLC
description: Whether sovereign immunity bars 2600 Holdings' claims for a writ of mandamus and declaratory judgment against state agencies regarding medical marijuana cultivation licenses.
plaintiff_argument: Sovereign immunity does not bar their request for a writ of mandamus, as it is constitutionally provided, nor does it bar their claim for declaratory relief, as the State's actions were illegal and unconstitutional, compelling the MMC to revoke a license and issue it to them and the ABC to enforce constitutional provisions.
defendant_argument: Sovereign immunity bars the complaint because 2600 Holdings seeks to control state agencies' administrative decisions, and the circuit court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction over the claims, especially for declaratory relief, as the APA does not permit judicial review of MMC's decision and 2600 Holdings failed to plead illegal or unconstitutional actions.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part the denial of the motion to dismiss the writ of mandamus claim, reversed in part the denial of the motion to dismiss the declaratory relief claim, and dismissed claims seeking relief under the APA for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.

title: Palade v. Board of Trustees of the University of Arkansas System
description: Whether the circuit court erred in dismissing the appellants' claims regarding the University of Arkansas System's revised faculty tenure policy on the grounds of lack of standing, unripeness, and nonjusticiability.
plaintiff_argument: The appellants, tenured faculty members, argued that the circuit court erred by dismissing their claims, asserting that the Revised Policy unilaterally and impermissibly modified their contractual and constitutional rights, and that their claims were justiciable and ripe for adjudication.
defendant_argument: The Board of Trustees argued that the appellants lacked standing, their claims were unripe and nonjusticiable, and that the Revised Policy merely clarified existing conduct standards without infringing on rights.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Arkansas affirmed the circuit court's dismissal of the appellants' claims, finding them nonjusticiable due to lack of standing and unripeness.

title: Rutledge v. Remmel
description: Whether the Attorney General exceeded her statutory authority and committed an illegal exaction by filing briefs in out-of-state litigation, spending public funds on consumer education advertisements, and engaging in partisan political activities, and whether she is immune from suit.
plaintiff_argument: The Attorney General exceeded her authority by filing briefs in national litigation without state interest, spent public funds on consumer education ads for self-promotion, and engaged in partisan activities, all constituting an illegal exaction.
defendant_argument: The Attorney General's actions were within her statutory authority, and she is protected by sovereign and statutory immunity, especially since plaintiffs failed to allege malicious acts for individual capacity claims.
decision_outcome: The court reversed and dismissed the claim for injunctive relief against the Attorney General in her official capacity and the illegal-exaction claim against her in her individual capacity, but dismissed the appeal regarding the illegal-exaction claim against her in her official capacity, remanding it for further proceedings.

title: Bentonville School District v. Sitton
description: Whether the Bentonville School District's mandatory mask policy for students violated parents' constitutional rights and whether the District had the authority to implement such a policy.
plaintiff_argument: The parents argued that the school district's mask policy violated their constitutional rights to care for their children and that the district lacked the legal authority to implement such a policy.
defendant_argument: The school district argued that its mask policy did not violate parents' constitutional rights, was within its authority to promote student health and safety, and that the parents failed to demonstrate irreparable harm.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's temporary restraining order that had enjoined the school district's mask policy and remanded the case.

title: Arkansas Department of Health v. Solomon
description: Whether the Arkansas Board of Hearing Instrument Dispensers violated Samuel Solomon's constitutional due process and equal protection rights by refusing to renew his license and denying a hearing, and whether the circuit court properly exercised jurisdiction and granted a preliminary injunction.
plaintiff_argument: The Board's refusal to provide proper renewal notice and a hearing violated his due process and equal protection rights under the Arkansas Constitution, and was an arbitrary and capricious abuse of power. He sought a preliminary injunction to prevent the State from refusing to renew his license.
defendant_argument: The circuit court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction, the lawsuit was barred by sovereign immunity, and the preliminary injunction exceeded the scope of relief available under Rule 65 and was not supported by the requisite findings.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's denial of the State's motion to dismiss regarding Solomon's due process claim, reversed and dismissed his equal protection claim, and reversed and remanded the preliminary injunction for the circuit court to make required findings.

title: Edwards v. Thomas
description: Whether Arkansas Code Annotated section 27-34-106(a) violates the separation-of-powers doctrine under article 4, section 2, and Amendment 80, section 3, of the Arkansas Constitution, with the plaintiff arguing it is a substantive rule of law and the defendant arguing it is procedural and thus unconstitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that Arkansas Code Annotated section 27-34-106(a) is a substantive rule of law and therefore does not violate the separation-of-powers doctrine.
defendant_argument: The defendant contended that Arkansas Code Annotated section 27-34-106(a) is procedural and thus unconstitutional as it violates the separation-of-powers doctrine.
decision_outcome: The court held that Arkansas Code Annotated section 27-34-106(a) is more substantive than procedural and does not violate the separation-of-powers doctrine.

title: McCarty v. Arkansas State Plant Board
description: Whether Arkansas Code Annotated § 2-16-206(a), which allows private entities to appoint members to the Arkansas State Plant Board, is an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that Arkansas Code Annotated § 2-16-206(a) is unconstitutional because it delegates legislative appointment power to private entities, violating the separation of powers.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that Arkansas Code Annotated § 2-16-206(a) is constitutional.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's finding, holding that Arkansas Code Annotated § 2-16-206(a) is unconstitutional and remanded with instructions to remove the unconstitutionally appointed Board members.

title: Thurston v. Safe Surgery Arkansas
description: Whether Arkansas Code Annotated section 7-9-601(b), which mandates that sponsors of initiative petitions obtain state and federal criminal background checks for paid canvassers from the Arkansas State Police and certify they passed, is unconstitutional because compliance is impossible, thereby infringing on the people's initiative and referenda rights.
plaintiff_argument: Safe Surgery Arkansas (SSA) argued that sections 7-9-601(b)(1) and (b)(3) are unconstitutional because it is impossible to obtain federal background checks from the Arkansas State Police (ASP) as required, making it impossible to certify that paid canvassers have passed such checks, thus violating Amendment 7's protection of initiative and referenda rights.
defendant_argument: Thurston argued that the circuit court lacked jurisdiction, that compliance with the statute was not impossible and could be achieved in various ways, and that the antifraud requirements served important state interests. Thurston also contended the preliminary injunction was overbroad.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's preliminary injunction, ruling that Arkansas Code Annotated section 7-9-601(b)(1) and (b)(3) are unconstitutional because it is impossible for initiative sponsors to comply with the federal background check requirements, and thus enjoined their enforcement.

title: Convent Corp. v. City of North Little Rock
description: Whether the City of North Little Rock's condemnation of Convent Corporation's property and its associated ordinances and procedures are constitutional and legally sound, particularly regarding due process, vagueness, and bills of attainder.
plaintiff_argument: Convent argued that the City's condemnation decision was not supported by substantial evidence, was arbitrary and capricious, violated due process (inadequate notice, meaningful hearing, opportunity to repair), its ordinances were unconstitutionally vague, and the resolution was an unlawful bill of attainder. Convent also contended that the circuit court erred by dismissing its constitutional, civil-rights, and trespass claims for failure to exhaust administrative remedies.
defendant_argument: The City argued that its condemnation decision was supported by substantial evidence, its procedures and ordinances were constitutional, Convent lacked standing, and Convent failed to exhaust administrative remedies for some claims. The City also asserted that Convent's vagueness claim was raised too late and the bill of attainder claim was invalid as the condemnation was an administrative, not legislative, act.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part (facial due-process claim, bill of attainder, vagueness, denial of motion to strike), reversed and remanded in part (dismissal of constitutional, civil-rights, and trespass claims for failure to exhaust administrative remedies, as-applied due-process claim), and dismissed as moot in part (administrative appeal of condemnation decision).
